drapeaux.note: "Knowledge of the law and exemplary probity" is the English rendering of the 1809 Instrument of Government given on the Parliamentary Ombudsmen's own history page (https://www.jo.se/en/about-jo/history/), which reads "a man known for his knowledge of the law and exemplary probity"; only the gender-neutral fragment is quoted. It is the Office's rendering, not a separately verified official translation of the Instrument.

"Extraordinary impact on opinion" (from a contemporary academic account, in the French) is back-translated into English; the original wording was not located. A possible source is Walter Gellhorn, Ombudsmen and Others: Citizens' Protectors in Nine Countries (1966), p. 6 (cited in PMC4311055), but the exact English was not found.

titre: A Swedish Invention That Stood Almost Alone for a Century and a Half
accroche: In 1809, Sweden invents a magistrate charged with watching its own officials on behalf of Parliament. Only one country copies the idea before 1950.
contenu_vulgarise:
In March 1809, a plot by officers deposes the King of Sweden, Gustav IV Adolf, while almost all of Finland, a Swedish province, has fallen into the hands of Russian troops. The new Constitution, adopted on June 6, does more than limit royal power: it creates a post that exists nowhere else yet, a magistrate charged with watching, on behalf of Parliament, how the administration applies the law.

## Neither judge nor minister

The king already had a Chancellor of Justice, a title borne since 1719 by the highest of the royal ombudsmen. What the Instrument of Government of 1809 invents is different: a *Justitieombudsman*, chosen by Parliament itself from among persons known for their “knowledge of the law and exemplary probity,” to give it its own eyes on how laws are applied by judges and officials alike. His role at first resembles that of a prosecutor: he inspects, investigates complaints, and may prosecute an official at fault before the courts. Lars Augustin Mannerheim is elected the first holder of the post in 1810.

The Swedish word *ombudsman* comes from an Old Norse term that simply means “representative.” The idea it designates today (an independent third party, appointed by an assembly, to whom a citizen can complain about an administration without going to trial) is already contained in this 1809 arrangement.

## A century and a half almost alone

No one takes up the idea for a hundred and ten years. Finland adopts it in 1919. Then nothing for more than three decades: the ombudsman remains a Scandinavian curiosity. Only with the Danish law of June 11, 1954 is a third office born, and in 1955 a jurist, Stephan Hurwitz, professor of criminal law at the University of Copenhagen, becomes its first holder.

## What tipped the idea

Hurwitz conducts a genuine campaign of explanation to make his office known abroad: his writings appear in Danish, English, French, German, and Italian. One intervention counts particularly: an interview given to the BBC has, according to a contemporary academic account, an “extraordinary impact on opinion” in Britain. Norway and New Zealand create their own ombudsman in 1962, the United Kingdom in 1967. Around 2001, according to the Slovenian ombudsman, the institution exists at the national level in about a hundred and ten countries.

The idea was a hundred and forty-five years old when Denmark made it the third office in history, and it is around its first holder that the campaign that made it known beyond Sweden and Finland is organized. The history of the ombudsman thus comes down to two dates separated by a long silence: 1809 for the invention, 1954 for the beginning of its spread.

repere.texte: In 1809, after the king's deposition, the new Swedish Constitution creates the post of Parliament's ombudsman, the first of its kind in the world: a magistrate charged with watching the administration on behalf of the elected members. It takes until 1919 for a second country, Finland, to adopt the idea.
repere.source: Instrument of Government (Regeringsformen), 1809; Parliamentary Ombudsmen (JO), History

carte.punch: The ombudsman is 145 years old when a third country, Denmark, adopts it.
carte.idee: In 1809, Sweden creates a magistrate appointed by Parliament to watch the administration. Finland copies the idea in 1919, then Denmark in 1954: its first holder, Stephan Hurwitz, then runs a campaign to make it known abroad.

quiz.question: After Sweden (1809) and Finland (1919), which country creates a third ombudsman office in 1954?
quiz.explication: Denmark adopts its law on June 11, 1954 and Stephan Hurwitz takes office in 1955. Norway and New Zealand follow in 1962, the United Kingdom in 1967.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what political context does Sweden create the parliamentary ombudsman post in 1809?
choix: After the deposition of King Gustav IV Adolf by a plot of officers, while Finland was occupied by Russia
After a peasant revolt demanding an end to royal taxes on harvests
Following a peace treaty with Denmark that imposed a constitutional reform
During the Napoleonic occupation of Sweden, on the orders of the French authorities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The new Swedish Constitution, adopted on June 6, 1809, follows the deposition of King Gustav IV Adolf in March by a plot of officers, whose immediate cause was the Russian occupation of Finland.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What power does the first Swedish ombudsman have over officials at fault?
choix: He can dismiss them directly, without going through a court
He can prosecute them before the courts, his initial role resembling that of a prosecutor
He can fine them, with the amount set by Parliament
He submits an annual report to the king, who alone decides on sanctions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the Riksdag, the role of the 1809 ombudsman could be characterized as that of a prosecutor: he inspects, investigates complaints, and prosecutes officials at fault before the courts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who leads the campaign that makes the ombudsman idea known abroad after 1954?
choix: A resolution adopted by the League of Nations in favor of its spread
The official translation of the Swedish Constitution of 1809 into several languages
An agreement among the Nordic countries to promote their institutions together
The Dane Stephan Hurwitz, first holder of the Danish office, whose BBC interview has an extraordinary impact
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first Danish ombudsman, Stephan Hurwitz, publishes in several languages and gives a BBC interview whose impact on British opinion is described as extraordinary by a contemporary academic account.
